How temple design changed

Follow Odisha's temples era by era — what changed, who built it, and which temples still show it.

  1. Era 1 of 6

    Rock-cut roots

    The Udayagiri and Khandagiri caves were cut into the rock in about the 2nd–1st century BCE. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [1]

    For curious grown-ups

    Percy Brown: the Orissan caves were cut within about 150 years before the Common Era; he reads a mean date of about 160 BCE from the Hathigumpha inscription.

    The Hathigumpha inscription tells of King Kharavela, ruler of Kalinga. He was a Jain, and he seems to have taken a special interest in the monks who lived in these hills. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [1]

    For curious grown-ups

    Percy Brown reads the Hathigumpha inscription this way. He writes that Kharavela 'was by religion a Jain, and appears to have been personally interested in the priestly community who had selected these hills as a place of retreat.'

    Before the temples

    These are not temples. They are monasteries: rooms cut into the rock for monks. The local name for them is gumpha (cave). Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [1]

    Temples from this era

    • Udayagiri and Khandagiri caves (incl. Rani Gumpha, Hathi Gumpha)

  2. Era 2 of 6

    First temples

    Experts still argue about the age of the earliest Bhubaneswar temples. One careful guess puts them between about 750 and 900 CE. Another says some are even older. Debated: sources disagree, or it rests on tradition. [1,2]

    For curious grown-ups

    Panigrahi places the Parasuramesvara group in the Shailodbhava period, which by his tentative chronology ended in the second half of the 8th century CE. Brown dates Parasuramesvara towards the end of the 8th century CE and his Early period to c. 750–900 CE.

    This was the time of the Shailodbhava kings, then the Bhauma-Kara kings. No one knows for certain which king built which temple here. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [2]

    For curious grown-ups

    K. C. Panigrahi: 'we do not know whether any of the Sailodbhava rulers was a builder of any of the temples here'; of the Bhauma-Karas, 'there is not a single tradition ... which connects any of the known rulers of the dynasty with any of its numerous existing monuments.'

    The early temples

    A basic Odisha temple has two buildings: the deul (shrine tower) and the jagamohana (front hall). Parasuramesvara has both. Its tower is still simple, short, sturdy and heavy, like a first draft. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [1]

    For curious grown-ups

    Percy Brown: two buildings 'combined constitute the essentials of the Orissan temple type'; he calls the Parasuramesvara tower's shape 'definitely rudimentary' and the temple itself 'inclined to be heavy and crude.'

    The Vaital Deul has a rounded, vaulted roof, like a barrel. Experts think this shape carries on from the roofs of old Buddhist chaitya (prayer) halls. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [1]

    For curious grown-ups

    Percy Brown saw this roof as a survival of the Buddhist chaitya-hall roof: 'its unmistakable vaulted roof occasionally survives in the Hindu temple, as for instance in ... the singularly interesting Vaital Deul.'

    Temples from this era

    • Parasuramesvara Temple
    • Vaital Deul

  3. Era 3 of 6

    Experiment & refinement

    From about 900 to 1100 CE, the Odisha style reached its early prime: its first high point. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [1]

    For curious grown-ups

    Percy Brown calls this his 'Middle Period', dating it 'cir. 900 to 1100 A.D.' and describing it as 'the movement at its early maturity or prime.'

    This was the age of the Somavamshi (Kesari) kings. Their dynasty was founded by King Janamejaya. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [2]

    For curious grown-ups

    K. C. Panigrahi: 'it was Janamejaya who founded the Somavamsi or Kesari dynasty of Kosala and Utkala.'

    A new polish

    Mukteshvara is a 'miniature gem' — highly finished, decorated with carved patterns, and reached through a torana (arched gateway). It is one of the few Odisha temples with carvings inside too. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [1]

    For curious grown-ups

    Percy Brown: Mukteshvara 'is a miniature gem of architecture ... highly finished structure, ornamented with fascinating carved patterns ... approached by an arched gateway, or torana', and 'one of the few temples of the Orissan group which has sculptured decoration in its interior.'

    Some experts think that art and building styles from the upper Mahanadi valley (old Kosala) travelled to Utkala (Odisha) — and helped start a revival of art there. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [2]

    For curious grown-ups

    K. C. Panigrahi argues this: 'we have shown how the art and architecture of the Upper Mahanadi Valley ... travelled to Utkala to initiate a revival of artistic conceptions.'

    Temples from this era

    • Mukteshvara Temple

  4. Era 4 of 6

    Monumental scale

    The Lingaraja temple is dated to about 1000 CE. The present Jagannath temple at Puri is dated to about 1100 CE. Debated: sources disagree, or it rests on tradition. [1,2]

    For curious grown-ups

    Percy Brown: Lingaraja c. 1000 CE; Jagannath about 1100 CE, 'not consecrated until' 1118 CE, and linked to 'Chora Ganga, the conqueror of Kalinga in 1030'. K. C. Panigrahi: Chodaganga's rule in Odisha is shown by a Lingaraja inscription of 1114 CE. Dates rest on style and later records.

    Somavamshi kings raised the greatest Shiva temple at Bhubaneswar. Later, the Ganga king Anantavarman Chodaganga conquered Utkala (Odisha). Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [2]

    For curious grown-ups

    K. C. Panigrahi: 'the kings of the dynasty were instrumental in raising the greatest Saiva temple at Bhubaneswar besides a number of smaller ones'; 'The direct connexion of the Gangas with Utkala or Orissa began with its conquest by Anantavarman Chodagangadeva.'

    Towers and halls

    The fully developed temple had four buildings in a line. In front of the jagamohana (front hall) came the natamandira (dance hall), then the bhogamandapa (hall of offerings). At Lingaraja these two halls were added later, probably a century or more after the rest. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [1]

    At Lingaraja the tower walls rise straight at first, then curve inward more and more toward the top. At Puri, the top of this curve is given a more graceful line. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [1]

    For curious grown-ups

    Percy Brown, on the shoulder curve at Puri: 'the overhang of the shoulder, which in this instance has been reduced to a more graceful line, giving its profile additional refinement and balance.'

    Temples from this era

    • Lingaraja Temple
    • Jagannath Temple, Puri

  5. Era 5 of 6

    Grand finale

    The Sun Temple at Konark was built in the 13th century CE, around the middle of that century. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [1,3]

    Not yet verified — see our content policy.

    The chariot of the Sun

    Konark's parts were all planned together as one design, unlike the separate buildings of Lingaraja and Jagannath. The whole temple is shaped like the chariot of Surya, the Sun god, with wheels and seven horses. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [1,3]

    For curious grown-ups

    Percy Brown: Konark is 'a reasoned and systematic co-ordination of its parts into an architectural unity', 'fashioned like a ratha or wheeled car being whirled along by the seven horses of the sun.' Seven horses follows Brown; the short UNESCO summary page says six.

    Konark's main tower has fallen, and only its foundations remain. The jagamohana (front hall) is the part that still stands fairly intact. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [1]

    Temples from this era

    • Konark Sun Temple

  6. Era 6 of 6

    Late Kalinga

    The Suryavamshi (Gajapati) kings ruled Odisha from the 15th century CE. Their power was already fading by the early 16th century CE, under King Prataparudra. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [2]

    For curious grown-ups

    Panigrahi gives Kapilendra's accession as 1435 CE on one page and his reign as 1433–1467 CE on another.

    The Suryavamshi (Gajapati) dynasty was founded by Kapilendra, once a Ganga officer. It produced two more able rulers, Purushottama and Prataparudra. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [2]

    Later temples

    The great age of temple building ended with the Gangas, though some notable temples were still built. The architectural style changed little, but sculpture declined. Scholarly view: experts' best reading of the clues. [2]

    For curious grown-ups

    K. C. Panigrahi: 'After the Gangas, the glorious period of temple-building activities in Orissa was over, but the spirit lingered on ... which also witnessed the erection of some notable temples'; 'the dynastic change did not result in any great change in architectural style, but in sculpture a definite set-back is to be perceived.'

    The Kapilesvara temple in Bhubaneswar may belong to this period, but no one is sure. Like the great Ganga temples, it has three halls in front of its shrine. Debated: sources disagree, or it rests on tradition. [2]

    For curious grown-ups

    Panigrahi dates it by style only. He says it 'seems to have belonged to this period' and 'appears to be the last notable monument' at Bhubaneswar. He says it stands on the site of an earlier temple. No second source was checked.

    Temples from this era

    • Kapilesvara Temple, Bhubaneswar
    • Papanasini temple porch (half-ruined), Bhubaneswar
